title: Pseudepigrapha in the New Testament
subtitle: Books written in another's name — the scholarly debate over New Testament authorship, the case of 2 Peter, and how two traditions police attribution
summary: Several New Testament letters name an apostle as author even though many scholars question that attribution. The strongest disputes concern letters such as 2 Peter and some Pauline epistles; other books remain widely accepted as authentic. The issue is not whether all Christian scripture is fabricated, but whether writings of uncertain authorship can bear the same claim of protected revelation as a publicly transmitted prophetic recitation.

seo.metaTitle: Pseudepigrapha in the New Testament: The 2 Peter Question
seo.metaDescription: Several New Testament letters name an apostle as author even though many scholars question that attribution.

sections.title: The Evidence in Brief
sections.body: Several New Testament letters name an apostle as author even though many scholars question that attribution. The strongest disputes concern letters such as 2 Peter and some Pauline epistles; other books remain widely accepted as authentic. The issue is not whether all Christian scripture is fabricated, but whether writings of uncertain authorship can bear the same claim of protected revelation as a publicly transmitted prophetic recitation.

sections.title: In Brief
sections.body: Pseudepigraphy means writing in another person’s name. Most scholars accept seven of Paul’s letters as genuine, seriously debate Ephesians, Colossians, and 2 Thessalonians, and regard the Pastoral Epistles as likely written after Paul. Second Peter is the clearest disputed case and was also received cautiously by parts of the early church. These are scholarly judgments, not proof that every New Testament book is falsely attributed. They do, however, raise an important question: should writings of uncertain authorship carry the same certainty as publicly transmitted revelation?

sections.title: Writing in Another’s Name in the Ancient World
sections.body:
Writing under a revered name was common in the ancient world, but scholars disagree about how audiences understood it. David Meade argues that some writers claimed continuity with a founder’s teaching rather than intending ordinary fraud. Bart Ehrman answers that ancient readers did recognize false attribution and often condemned it.

The early church rejected some works because it judged their apostolic names false. Serapion of Antioch rejected the Gospel of Peter on that basis, and the Muratorian Fragment rejects letters attributed falsely to Paul. Second Thessalonians 2:1-2 also warns about a letter presented as apostolic, while 3:17 gives a handwritten sign of authenticity. Whether Second Thessalonians itself is Pauline remains debated, but the warning shows that false apostolic attribution was a real concern, not a category invented by modern critics.

sections.title: The Three Tiers of the Pauline Letters
sections.body:
The thirteen letters bearing Paul’s name fall into three broad groups. Romans, 1-2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon are accepted as Pauline by almost all scholars. Ephesians, Colossians, and 2 Thessalonians are genuinely disputed. Most critical scholars date 1-2 Timothy and Titus after Paul.

The doubts involve vocabulary, writing style, church organization, theology, and difficulty fitting the letters into Paul’s known life. Conservative scholars reply that topic, age, coauthors, or secretaries can explain differences and that Paul may have ministered after the imprisonment described in Acts. The majority judgment is significant, but it remains a historical conclusion open to argument—not a mathematical proof.

sections.title: The Case of 2 Peter: The Critical Argument
sections.body:
Second Peter is the New Testament book most often judged pseudonymous. Its Greek differs sharply from 1 Peter; much of Jude appears in reworked form; the letter answers concern about Christ’s delayed return; and 2 Peter 3:15-16 appears to know a collection of Paul’s letters already treated as Scripture. Many scholars therefore date it after Peter’s death, often around 100-150 CE.

These arguments converge but are not equally decisive. Different style can have more than one cause, literary borrowing does not prove a late date, and 'the fathers' in 3:4 could refer to the patriarchs. Richard Bauckham accepts a late first-century setting but reads the work as a literary testament rather than a deceptive letter. The critical case is strong enough to matter, while its precise date and intention remain debated.

sections.title: The Conservative Case for 2 Peter
sections.body:
Defenders of Petrine authorship offer substantial replies. Peter may have used different secretaries, which could explain the change in Greek style. Jude may have borrowed from Second Peter, or both may depend on shared material. 'The fathers' can mean Old Testament patriarchs rather than a dead Christian generation. Limited early citation may reflect the letter’s short length and circulation rather than a late origin.

Second Peter 1:16 explicitly presents its author as an eyewitness. Defenders take that statement at face value and argue that a church alert to false attribution would not knowingly canonize a fabricated claim. Critics answer that strong self-authentication is exactly what pseudonymous writing requires. The defense deserves to be heard, but it does not erase why so many specialists and some early Christians hesitated over the book.

sections.title: An Islamic Lens: Writing a Text and Calling It God’s
sections.body:
Quran 2:79 condemns people who write a text and then say, 'This is from Allah.' The verse addresses particular misconduct, not a named New Testament book, but it establishes a clear Islamic principle: words attributed to God or His messengers require trustworthy transmission.

The Quran’s history presents a strong contrast. It was recited publicly, memorized, written during the Prophet’s life, collected soon after his death, and standardized within the first Muslim generation by named participants. Quran 15:9 also declares God’s protection of the revelation. There is no Quranic book whose claimed prophetic author is rejected by most specialists.

Muslims also confronted fabricated hadith. Rather than place every report inside an ungraded canon, scholars recorded chains of transmission, investigated narrators, compared routes and wording, and graded reports from authentic to fabricated. This does not make every hadith certain. It shows that Islam distinguished the mass-transmitted Quran from reports requiring individual authentication and built tools to expose false attribution.

sections.title: Where Each Tradition Locates Its Guaranteed Core
sections.body:
The central difference is where each tradition locates certainty. Christianity places disputed-attribution books inside the New Testament canon. Conservative Christians defend their traditional authorship; other Christians say inspiration belongs to the text recognized by the church even if the named writer is uncertain. The difficulty is that the early church itself sometimes rejected books because it believed their apostolic names were false.

Islam locates its guaranteed scripture in one publicly recited Quran transmitted within the first generation. Hadith remain authoritative when authenticated, but individual reports are openly graded and can be rejected without removing a verse from the Quran. Christians may reply that knowledge of Quranic compilation also comes through reports. Muslims answer that those reports agree with mass recitation, early manuscripts, and the absence of a rival Quranic text.

This comparison does not prove that every disputed Christian book is false. It does show why the Islamic preservation model offers firmer public grounds for identifying revelation: the Quran is early, communal, textually stable, and separate from the graded reports surrounding it.

sections.title: Why This Matters: Pseudepigrapha in the New Testament
sections.body: Several New Testament letters carry apostolic names that many scholars question, especially Second Peter and the Pastoral Epistles. Serious conservative defenses remain, so the evidence should not be exaggerated into a claim that the whole New Testament is forged. The comparison still favors Islam’s preservation model: a public Quran transmitted within one generation, alongside a separate hadith tradition whose reports are named, tested, and graded rather than automatically treated as scripture.

faq.question: What exactly does “pseudepigrapha” mean?
faq.answer: From Greek, it means “falsely inscribed” writings — works composed by one person but circulated under the name of another, usually a revered figure. In New Testament studies the term (or “pseudonymity”) describes the scholarly view that some canonical books carry apostolic names their actual authors did not bear.

faq.question: Do all scholars agree that 2 Peter was not written by Peter?
faq.answer: No. Most critical scholars judge it pseudonymous — J. N. D. Kelly’s line that “scarcely anyone nowadays doubts” it is often quoted — but the verdict is contested. Michael Kruger, E. M. B. Green, and the textbook of Carson and Moo defend Petrine authorship, and Richard Bauckham holds a mediating view: a late-first-century “testament” whose original readers would have recognized the genre.

faq.question: If the early church doubted 2 Peter, why is it in the Bible?
faq.answer: The doubts were eventually weighed and set aside: Athanasius’s Easter letter of 367 and the late-fourth-century councils received it among the seven Catholic Epistles. Defenders read that history as evidence of careful scrutiny rather than credulity; critical scholars read it as a late decision made without the linguistic and historical tools available today. Both readings of the same facts are represented in current scholarship.

faq.question: Which Pauline letters does mainstream scholarship consider genuine?
faq.answer: Seven are undisputed: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon. Ephesians, Colossians, and 2 Thessalonians are seriously disputed, with scholars on both sides. Most critical scholars regard the Pastorals (1-2 Timothy, Titus) as written in Paul’s name after his death — a majority view that conservative scholarship contests in detail.

faq.question: Does Islam have an equivalent problem of false attribution?
faq.answer: False attribution occurred in hadith literature, and Muslim scholars said so openly. The difference is structural: fabricated or weak hadith are not part of the Quran and can be rejected through hadith criticism without removing a verse from scripture. The Quran was a public recitation collected and standardized in the first generation, with early manuscript and mass-transmission evidence. Islam therefore has a serious history of disputed reports, but not a direct equivalent of a canonical Quranic chapter that most specialists attribute to someone other than its claimed apostolic author.

faq.question: If a biblical book is pseudonymous, does that make it worthless or Christianity false?
faq.answer: Not by itself. A pseudonymity verdict is a historical judgment about human authorship, and Christian theologians hold a range of positions on how inspiration relates to that question — from denying the verdicts outright to arguing that canonical authority does not depend on modern authorship verification. What the debate does affect is the argument that canonicity guarantees apostolic authorship; each reader must weigh how much rests on that link.

furtherReading.title: Forgery and Counterforgery: The Use of Literary Deceit in Early Christian Polemics
furtherReading.author: Bart D. Ehrman
furtherReading.note: The fullest modern statement of the critical case that early Christian pseudepigraphy was forgery in the ancient world’s own terms.

furtherReading.title: Jude, 2 Peter (Word Biblical Commentary 50)
furtherReading.author: Richard Bauckham
furtherReading.note: The standard technical commentary; argues for a first-century date and reads 2 Peter as a “testament” whose pseudonymity was a transparent convention.

furtherReading.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
furtherReading.author: D. A. Carson and Douglas J. Moo
furtherReading.note: The leading conservative textbook; defends traditional authorship of the disputed letters, including 2 Peter and the Pastorals.
